## A mixed subgroup table

`RESPIRE` reports both subgroups in every trial. `steroids` does not.
CoDEX, DEXA-COVID 19, and
RECOVERY contribute only **IV** (invasively ventilated patients). The
other four trials contribute both IV and NIV (non-invasive support;
Sterne, Murthy et al. 2020).

Those IV-only trials can inform an IV treatment effect. They do not
contain a within-trial IV-versus-NIV contrast, so they cannot identify
the interaction \(g_j=y_{\mathrm{IV},j}-y_{\mathrm{NIV},j}\).

This vignette contrasts Difference of Averages (DA), Average Difference
(AD), Same Weighting Across Different Analyses (SWADA), and
contribution-adjusted meta-analysis (CAMS) on that mixed table. DA, AD,
and SWADA are **different constructions**, not alternative CAMS models
(`vignette("consistent-interactions")`). The CAMS map itself is
`vignette("cams")`. The fit here uses frequentist CAMS.

```{r load}
library(interactmeta)
```

```{r steroids-pattern}
st <- steroids[steroids$n > 0, ]
table(st$trial, st$subgroup)
```

## Missing cells in CAMS

CAMS keeps the IV-only trials. The missing NIV cell is filled with
a nearly uninformative placeholder (`yi = 0`, `vi = 100^2`). The trial
then sits at \(\pi_j\approx 1\) in the overall block and is essentially
silent in the interaction block.

DA, AD, and SWADA need both cells in every trial. Complete the table
once, then fit all four with **metafor** so the comparison is
like-for-like. Mortality odds ratios (ORs) are built from the 2×2
counts.

```{r steroids-fit, cache = TRUE}
steroids_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = treat.events,
  bi = treat.total - treat.events,
  ci = cont.events,
  di = cont.total - cont.events,
  data = st
)
des <- ifrac(steroids_es, reference = "NIV")
fit_da_st <- da(des, reference = "NIV")
fit_ad_st <- ad(des, reference = "NIV")
fit_sw_st <- swada(des, reference = "NIV")
fit_cams_st <- cam(des, reference = "NIV", engine = "metafor")
```

```{r steroids-des-print}
head(des)
```

## Where the interaction comes from

The interaction is identified by the complete trials. Under default
interaction random-effects (RE) weights, AD, SWADA, and CAMS
\(\gamma\) agree. DA does not: it still uses the IV-only trials in the
IV series.

```{r steroids-int}
compare_interactions(
  fit_da_st,
  fit_ad_st,
  fit_sw_st,
  fit_cams_st,
  exponentiate = TRUE
)
```

```{r steroids-weights}
compare_weights(fit_da_st, fit_ad_st, fit_sw_st)
```

RECOVERY and CoDEX take a large share of the DA **IV** weights and
essentially none of the AD/SWADA weights. That is the SWADA principle
on a mixed table: shared interaction weights silence trials that do
not identify \(g_j\).

## The two pooled information fractions

Trial \(\pi_j\) is design and does not change. What can change is the
reporting mix \(\omega=\sum_j\pi_j w_j/\sum_j w_j\).

The package default `ifrac = "interaction"` is the interaction
information fraction. The weights are the interaction-block
inverse-variance weights

$$
w_j=\frac{1}{\tau_\gamma^2+\mathrm{Var}(g_j)},
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(g_j)=\sigma_{Aj}^2+\sigma_{Bj}^2.
$$

`ifrac = "overall"` is the overall information fraction (IF)
(Panaro, Röver and Friede 2025, eq. 3.16). The weights are the
overall-block inverse-variance weights

$$
w_j=\frac{1}{\tau^2+v_j},
\qquad
v_j=\mathrm{Var}(m_j)=(1-\pi_j)^2\sigma_{Aj}^2+\pi_j^2\sigma_{Bj}^2.
$$

```{r steroids-ifrac-overall}
ifrac(fit_cams_st, ifrac = "overall")
```

```{r steroids-ifrac-interaction}
ifrac(fit_cams_st, ifrac = "interaction")
```

The two \(\omega\) differ because the IV-only trials dominate one
weighting and are silent in the other. They sit at \(\pi_j\approx 1\)
with \(\mathrm{Var}(m_j)\approx\sigma_{\mathrm{IV},j}^2\), so RECOVERY
in particular pulls overall \(\omega\) toward 1. The same trials have
\(\mathrm{Var}(g_j)\approx 100^2\), so interaction \(\omega\) is a
reweighting of the **complete** trials only.

Switching `ifrac` does not change a trial's \(\pi_j\) and does not
refit \(\gamma\). It changes which trials dominate the reporting mix
used by `subgroups()`, `combined()`, and `forestplot()`.

```{r steroids-forest-overall, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8}
forestplot(
  fit_cams_st,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  ifrac = "overall"
)
```

Overall and Prediction at the overall mix.

```{r steroids-forest-interaction, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8}
forestplot(
  fit_cams_st,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  ifrac = "interaction"
)
```

Overall and Prediction at the interaction mix.

```{r steroids-sg-overall}
subgroups(fit_cams_st, exponentiate = TRUE, ifrac = "overall")
```

```{r steroids-sg-interaction}
subgroups(fit_cams_st, exponentiate = TRUE, ifrac = "interaction")
```

If \(\omega\) is meant to represent the trials that identify the
treatment-by-subgroup interaction, `ifrac = "interaction"` matches
that block. At that mix the CAMS subgroup odds ratios sit next to
SWADA. DA's IV odds ratio does not: that series is still using the
IV-only trials. The `il6` table is the same incomplete-table pattern
on concomitant corticosteroids.

## Summary

Single-subgroup trials can inform a subgroup-specific treatment effect
without informing the within-trial interaction. AD, SWADA, and CAMS
base \(\gamma\) on complete trials. DA can still use single-subgroup
trials in a subgroup-specific series.

In CAMS, `ifrac = "overall"` versus `ifrac = "interaction"` changes
the pooled information fraction \(\omega\) used for
contribution-dependent summaries. It does not change the fitted
interaction. On a mixed table the two mixes differ because
single-subgroup trials can dominate \(\mathrm{Var}(m_j)\) weights and
are silent in \(\mathrm{Var}(g_j)\) weights.

## References

Panaro RV, Röver C, Friede T (2026). Subgroup comparisons within and
across studies in meta-analysis. *Research Synthesis Methods* (in
press). arXiv:2508.15531.

Panaro RV, Röver C, Friede T (2025). Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis
on subgroup specific effects and interactions. arXiv:2512.18785.

WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working
Group, Sterne JAC, Murthy S, et al. (2020). Association between
administration of systemic corticosteroids and mortality among
critically ill patients with COVID-19: a meta-analysis. *JAMA*,
324(13), 1330--1341.
